title: The London Tube map works because it ignores geography
body: In 1931 Harry Beck, a London Underground employee, drew the network as a diagram rather than a map: lines run only vertically, horizontally or at 45 degrees, and stations sit at even spacing regardless of real distances. London Underground was sceptical of his spare-time project, tried it in a small pamphlet in 1933, and it was an immediate hit. Beck was paid **ten guineas** for the card edition and five more for the poster. The look resembles an electrical circuit diagram, though circuits were not his inspiration, and metro maps worldwide have copied the style since.

left.label: Geographic map
left.text: True distances and directions, but the crowded centre becomes a tangle of lines.

right.label: Beck’s diagram
right.text: Only vertical, horizontal and 45° lines, evenly spaced stations, distances ignored: easy to read at a glance.

slides.question: How much was Beck paid for the first card edition of his map?
slides.explanation: Just ten guineas, roughly £650 in 2025 money, plus five guineas for the poster. He kept redesigning the map until 1960.

slides.label: Beck’s fee for the first card edition of the map, plus five for the poster
slides.text: About £650 in 2025 money for the card. The design has been emulated by underground systems around the world.

events.text: A small pamphlet tests it on the public
Sydney’s map is nearly a clone of London’s

slides.heading: Not a circuit
slides.text: A popular story says Beck borrowed the look from electrical circuit diagrams. The approach is similar, but circuits were not the inspiration for his map. Underground, a passenger needs the sequence of stations and the changes, not the geography above.
